quote: I am not going to tell you that it’s okay for you to not understand quantum mechanics, because no one understands quantum mechanics, as Richard Feynman once claimed. There was a historical time when this was true, but we no longer live in that era.
content: The era ended, on the essay’s account, with decoherence and Everett. The sequence’s own final essay admits that the Born probabilities, the only point at which the formalism touches experiment, have “no known reason” under that account; the standard reference on decoherence states that decoherence by itself “does not solve the measurement problem” (Schlosshauer (2005)); and the Everettian derivations of the Born rule that exist are decision-theoretic arguments whose premises are disputed by the field’s own participants (Kent, Albert and Price in Saunders et al., Many Worlds?, 2010, a volume with no single DOI; the essay’s author says in Many Worlds, One Best Guess that he is “rather suspicious” of them). So what the reader is promised, an explanation with no residual confusion, is achieved by deferring the unsolved part to the last essay and treating everything before it as settled. Feynman’s remark was not about the mathematics, which he understood better than anyone; it was about exactly the residue this sequence defers. A presentation that is clear until the point where the field is confused, and then confused in the same place, has not left the era; it has rearranged the syllabus.

quote: Dragging a modern-day student through all this may be a historically realistic approach to the subject matter, but it also ensures the historically realistic outcome of total bewilderment. Talking to aspiring young physicists about “wave/particle duality” is like starting chemistry students on the Four Elements.
content: The pedagogical claim is testable and has been studied, without support for the essay’s confidence. The physics-education literature on quantum mechanics finds that student difficulties with superposition, measurement and probability persist across curricula, including the “spins-first” and postulates-first sequences (McIntyre, Sakurai) that dispense with the historical order, and that no ordering has been shown to remove them (Krijtenburg-Lewerissa et al. (2017), a review of the field). The essay’s own alternative, amplitudes flowing between discrete configurations, is a simplification that the editors had to correct in a footnote (the phase convention for a beam splitter) and that omits normalization, as the annotation on the next essay records; it is not obvious that a student who learns it will be less confused when they meet the Hilbert-space formalism than one who learned about wave–particle duality first. The Four Elements comparison is also unfair to the history: wave–particle duality is not a superseded theory but a description of the phenomena that any interpretation must reproduce, and the double-slit experiment with single electrons (Tonomura et al., 1989) is still the cleanest demonstration of what the formalism is for.

quote: It is not only my view. It is probably the majority view among theoretical physicists, if that counts for anything (though I will argue the matter separately from opinion polls).
content: It is not the majority view, and it was not in 2008. The polls that exist put Everett at a minority of foundations-conference attendees: 18% in the 2011 survey of Schlosshauer, Kofler & Zeilinger (2013), against 42% for Copenhagen, with information-based and QBist views ahead of it; an informal poll by Tegmark in 1997 found under a third; a 2016 survey of physicists at large found the Everett share in single digits. Opus’s annotation on the sequence’s final essay gives the same figures. The essay hedges (“if that counts for anything”) and then, five essays later, in If Many-Worlds Had Come First, upgrades to “may now be the majority viewpoint (or not),” and the sequence’s tone throughout is that of someone speaking for a silent majority (“on behalf of any and all physicists out there who dare not say it themselves”). The realist reading of quantum mechanics, which the sentence also claims, is held by many physicists who are not Everettians, since Bohmians and collapse theorists are realists too; the essay uses “realist” and “many-worlds” as if they were one position.
